claims.text: A hybrid framework combining a machine-learning interatomic potential with periodic on-the-fly ab initio corrections can capture vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling in both solid and liquid states near melting.
The hybrid framework will substantially reduce the cost of computing fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties in multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The intended target includes elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy materials near solid–liquid coexistence.
Extensive explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics sampling will be replaced by a machine-learned potential trained on a dense set of configurations near the melting boundary.
Periodic ab initio corrections will preserve detailed vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration free-energy contributions.
The method will first be validated on elemental and binary systems and then extended to high-entropy alloys.
An interatomic-potential surrogate can act as a fast proxy for an ab initio potential-energy surface in a multicomponent high-entropy alloy.
Periodic ab initio updates can correct fidelity losses in the surrogate potential.
Sampling with the machine-learning surrogate drastically reduces the number of expensive ab initio molecular-dynamics steps.
Recalibrating the energy surface with periodic ab initio calculations ensures accurate treatment of vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
The proposed correction mechanism maintains accurate solid and liquid free energies near fusion.
The hybrid method is expected to reduce computational cost by approximately one order of magnitude relative to full ab initio molecular dynamics.
The hybrid method is expected to reproduce interphase free-energy differences within a few meV per atom.
The resulting melting temperatures and latent heats will closely agree with explicit ab initio evaluations.
The hybrid method will outperform TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
Existing explicit ab initio free-energy methods and TOR-TILD are accurate for elemental and binary systems but become prohibitively expensive or inefficient for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Performance may degrade under extreme anharmonicity when such configurations are insufficiently represented in the training data.
Failure to obtain a 5- to 10-fold speed-up or phase-free-energy errors below a few meV per atom relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics would falsify the hypothesis.
